blocks.text:
The first half of the day is free. It is best to save your energy for the nighttime parade, which lasts until morning.

In the evening, a transfer takes you to the Sambadrome. Carnival here feels very different from the photographs. You hear the drums before the first samba school even appears; the spectators rise in the stands as rows of performers enter the avenue, and enormous floats pass right before your eyes.

The Sambadrome is designed as a long avenue with grandstands on both sides. Samba schools parade along it one after another, each with a limited time to complete its performance. Behind the exuberant celebrations is meticulous coordination: musicians, dancers, floats and costumed groups must move as one. From the stands, it is a continuous succession of scenes, colours and music.

Each samba school creates its own theme, music, costumes and decorations. Months of preparation culminate in a single procession along the Sambadrome. Under the bright lights, you can pick out embroidery, feathers, sparkling details, elaborate headdresses and the complex structures of the floats.

You can feel the music: the percussion sections set the pace, the crowd's voices blend with the musicians, and the long procession never seems to pause. Light catches the sequins and gems on the costumes, towering floats partly obscure the stands, and each new school completely transforms the scene on the avenue.

The parade continues through the night. When it finishes, a transfer back to the hotel is provided. After so much light, music and movement, not everyone finds it easy to fall asleep straight away.

blocks.text:
After breakfast, set out on an approximately four-hour excursion to Corcovado.

The ascent begins aboard a train that travels through Tijuca Forest. Almost immediately, the windows frame dense treetops, vines and damp tree trunks, while the city gradually drops away below.

Tijuca Forest accompanies much of the climb. Damp trunks, broad leaves and vines flicker past the train windows, making the journey to the main lookout an experience in itself. After yesterday's open views from Sugar Loaf, Corcovado reveals Rio from another angle: both the ocean and the green expanses within the metropolis stretch out below.

At the summit stands the statue of Christ the Redeemer. Up close, it feels quite different from the way it looks from the city's streets: the figure towers above the viewing terrace, with a sweeping panorama of Rio beyond.

From the lookout you can see Guanabara Bay, the Rio–Niterói Bridge, Sugar Loaf, the Botanical Garden and Maracanã Stadium. Your English-speaking guide will tell you about the statue and the national park through which the route passes.

After the excursion, return to the city. The remaining time is yours to relax before your flight to Iguazu.

Corcovado brings the Rio de Janeiro section of the itinerary to a close with another remarkable panorama. In four days, you have seen the city from the beach, from Sugar Loaf, in the old town, at night in the Sambadrome and from the heights of Christ the Redeemer. Each viewpoint offers a different perspective on the same city and shows why Rio's dramatic landscape is such an essential part of the experience.
